base-pinned.name: Dockerfile base images are pinned
base-pinned.description: Every image a Dockerfile builds from is pinned to a digest, so rebuilding the same commit starts from the same bytes.
base-pinned.remediation:
Pin the image to the digest its tag points to today, so the base can't change between rebuilds:

```dockerfile
FROM node:20.11.1-alpine@sha256:e4b0d6d6b1a2c2a58e8dd8a0e0b1f0d0c2c9f9c5b3a1e0d9c8b7a6f5e4d3c2b1 AS build
```

Run `docker buildx imagetools inspect node:20.11.1-alpine` to print the digest to paste in. Renovate and Dependabot both raise pull requests to update a pinned digest, so the pin stays maintained instead of frozen.

A tag moves whenever the publisher pushes. Two builds of the same commit then produce different images, and the one an auditor asks about is not the one that ran.

allowTags.description: Whether a tag other than `latest` counts as a pin. `false` requires a digest, the only kind of reference that resolves to the same image every time.

registries.description: Comma separated registries an image may come from, such as `docker.io,ghcr.io`. Empty means any registry. An image naming no registry comes from Docker Hub, so name `docker.io` to allow those.

nonroot-user.name: Dockerfiles run as a non-root user
nonroot-user.description: Every Dockerfile ends with a `USER` that is not root, so the container runs its process without privileges.
nonroot-user.remediation:
Create an unprivileged user in the image and switch to it before the entrypoint:

```dockerfile
RUN addgroup -S app && adduser -S -G app app
USER app
```

The container runs as the last `USER` in the file, so a Dockerfile that declares none runs as uid 0. When a container starts as root, a bug in the application becomes a root-level problem on the host: mounted paths are writable, capabilities can be granted, and an escape lands somewhere that matters.

If the process needs a low port such as 80, publish a high port to it (`docker run -p 80:8080`) instead of staying root to bind 80.

no-build-secrets.name: Dockerfiles declare no credential arguments
no-build-secrets.description: No `ARG` or `ENV` declared in a Dockerfile has a name that looks like a credential.
no-build-secrets.remediation:
Pass the credential in at build time with a secret mount, which leaves nothing behind in the image:

```dockerfile
RUN --mount=type=secret,id=npm_token \
    NPM_TOKEN=$(cat /run/secrets/npm_token) npm ci
```

```bash
docker build --secret id=npm_token,env=NPM_TOKEN .
```

An `ARG` is recorded in the image history, and `docker history` prints it. An `ENV` stays in the image, and `docker inspect` prints it. Either way, anyone who can pull the image can read the value, and once a value has reached a registry you have to rotate it, because deleting it is not enough.

This guardrail only sees names, never values: the collector records neither the default next to an `ARG` nor the value next to an `ENV`. A name containing `TOKEN` is reason enough to rotate the credential.

patterns.description: Comma separated glob patterns, matched case-insensitively against the name of every `ARG` and every `ENV`. Only names are matched, because the collector records no values, which is what makes these facts safe to attach to a build.

healthcheck.name: Dockerfiles declare a health check
healthcheck.description: Every Dockerfile declares a `HEALTHCHECK`, so the orchestrator can tell a container that is running from one that is actually working.
healthcheck.remediation:
Add a `HEALTHCHECK` to the Dockerfile that probes what the container exists to do, not just whether the process is alive:

```dockerfile
HEALTHCHECK --interval=30s --timeout=3s --start-period=20s \
  CMD curl -fsS http://localhost:8080/health || exit 1
```

Without one, the runtime only knows that PID 1 hasn't exited. A process that is deadlocked, out of connections or serving 500s stays in the load balancer's rotation until somebody notices.

If you deploy to Kubernetes, a `readinessProbe` in the manifest does the same job and is a complete answer on its own, because the probe lives in the manifest instead of the image. List those Dockerfiles in `ignore`, which is matched as a glob against the path:

```json
{ "use": "docker/healthcheck@v1", "with": { "ignore": "deploy/k8s/*/Dockerfile" } }
```

Also list images that run a job and exit there, since they are meant to stop and have nothing to keep reporting on.

finalStageOnly.description: Whether only the last stage in the file is checked. A build stage is thrown away and never runs, so it has nothing to health check.

ignore.description: Comma separated globs naming Dockerfiles to skip, such as one that only ever builds a job image.

lint-clean.name: Dockerfile lint findings are clean
lint-clean.description: Every finding the Dockerfile linter reported is below the severity your team gates on.
lint-clean.remediation:
Fix the findings listed in the violations, or deliberately disable a rule in `.hadolint.yaml` where it doesn't apply:

```yaml
ignored:
  - DL3008
```

Run the linter in your build before this guardrail, so there is a report to read:

```bash
hadolint --format sarif Dockerfile > hadolint.sarif
```

The guardrail reads the report and never reruns the linter, so it judges the same findings your build acted on.

severity.description: Lowest severity that counts as a violation, on the scale the collector normalises every report to. Findings below it are logged, not reported. One of `critical`, `high`, `medium`, `low`, `info`.

ignore.description: Comma separated rule ids that are never a violation, such as `DL3008,DL3059`.
